name: FlashQLA
baseline: FLA Triton kernels (flash-linear-attention chunk_gated_delta_rule) and FlashInfer GDN prefill kernel
workload: Gated DeltaNet (GDN) chunked-prefill forward and backward kernels at Qwen3.5/Qwen3.6 head configurations (TP1 to TP8, d=128), single-sequence and varlen batches up to 32768 tokens, CUDA-graph timing on H200 and GB200.
claimed_speedup: README: '2-3x forward speedup and 2x backward speedup over the FLA Triton kernel'. benchmark_results_H200.txt, forward, 397B/122B TP8, 1x32768: FlashQLA 0.348 ms vs FLA 1.019 ms (2.93x) vs FlashInfer 1.645 ms (4.73x); 1x4096: 1.19x vs FLA; TP4 4096x8: 3.18x vs FLA but 0.64x vs FlashInfer. Across the 171 forward rows: 1.18x to 3.32x vs FLA (geometric mean 2.07x, derived from page data); across the 32 backward rows: 1.38x to 5.47x vs FLA (geometric mean 2.56x, derived from page data).
compiler_and_flags: torch 2.8.0+cu128, fla 0.5.1, flashinfer 0.6.13, tilelang 0.1.12; Warmup=10, Repeats=100, Backend=cudagraph (README text names FLA 0.5.0, Triton 3.5.1, FlashInfer 0.6.9, TileLang 0.1.8). No compiler flags stated.
hardware: NVIDIA H200 (benchmark_results_H200.txt) and NVIDIA GB200 (benchmark_results_GB200.txt); host CPU not stated
tradeoffs: Specific to Gated DeltaNet chunked prefill (Qwen3.5/3.6 linear-attention layers), not general attention. Needs Hopper or Blackwell GPUs (SM120 forward only) and the TileLang toolchain. Uses an algebraic reformulation of the GDN forward/backward flow that the authors say keeps numerical precision.
caveats: First-party benchmark; host CPU and compiler flags not stated, which is why this is tier C rather than A (benchmark script benchmark/bench_gated_delta_rule.py and the result files are public, so a verifier may be able to re-tier). Baselines are the FLA Triton and FlashInfer GDN kernels, not oneDNN/cuDNN/XNNPACK/Eigen. Speedup is shape dependent: forward 1.18x to 3.32x vs FLA, and FlashInfer is faster than FlashQLA in 56 of the 171 forward rows (as low as 0.62x, mostly small-batch varlen rows). Row statistics were computed from the H200 result file; the GB200 file was not parsed.
found_via: GitHub (search_repositories): 'flash attention kernel' sorted by stars, then README Benchmark section and benchmark/ directory

name: FlashKDA
baseline: flash-linear-attention (fla) Triton chunk_kda kernel, and fla chunk_gated_delta_rule (GDN) as a second reference
workload: Kimi Delta Attention (KDA) forward pass, T=8192, H=96 and H=64, D=128, fixed-length and variable-length batches, on Hopper H20 and Blackwell GB200.
claimed_speedup: BENCHMARK_H20.md (T=8192, H=96, D=128): flash_kda 2.6220 ms vs fla_chunk_kda 4.8388 ms (1.85x) fixed; 2.06x and 2.29x for the two varlen cases; H=64: 1.95x, 1.91x, 2.31x. BENCHMARK_GB200.md (H=96): 2.31x fixed, 2.71x and 3.27x varlen. Versus fla GDN kernel only 1.17x to 1.80x.
compiler_and_flags: warmup=30, iters=200, repeats=5; fla_chunk_kda with use_gate_in_kernel=True, use_qk_l2norm_in_kernel=True, use_beta_sigmoid_in_kernel=True, lower_bound=-5, transpose_state_layout=True; generated by benchmarks/generate_benchmark_hopper_h20_md.py; requires CUDA 12.9+, SM90+, PyTorch 2.4+. fla and PyTorch versions used for the numbers are not stated on the benchmark pages.
hardware: NVIDIA H20 (Hopper) in BENCHMARK_H20.md, generated 2026-04-22; NVIDIA GB200 (Blackwell) in BENCHMARK_GB200.md, generated 2026-05-26; host CPU not stated
stars_or_usage: 1.3k stars; auto-dispatched as a backend by flash-linear-attention's chunk_kda
tradeoffs: KDA forward only (the benchmark pages cover forward); requires SM90 or newer GPUs and CUDA 12.9+; uses bf16 inputs and a custom forward-substitution inverse, so results are checked against fla_chunk_kda for accuracy.
caveats: First-party benchmark with no software versions or CPU model on the benchmark pages. H20 is a low-compute, high-bandwidth SKU, so H20 numbers may not transfer to H100. Baseline is the FLA Triton KDA kernel, not oneDNN/cuDNN/XNNPACK/Eigen. Only the forward pass is benchmarked.
found_via: GitHub (search_repositories): 'flash attention kernel' sorted by stars, then root files BENCHMARK_H20.md and BENCHMARK_GB200.md

name: QuACK (CuTe-DSL memory-bound kernels)
baseline: cuDNN v9.10.1 (RMSNorm only), torch.compile (PyTorch 2.7.1, default mode) and Liger Kernel v0.5.10
workload: Memory-bound kernels (RMSNorm, softmax, cross-entropy; forward and backward), batch 8k to 32k rows, reduction dimension 256 to 262k, FP32 and BF16 inputs, measured as model memory throughput on H100.
claimed_speedup: Blog: 'achieves nearly 50% more throughput (e.g., 3.01 TB/s vs 1.89 TB/s for FP32 softmax)' than torch.compile at reduction dim 262k; about 3 TB/s (~90% of peak) for reduction dim larger than 4k; 'significantly outperforms all baselines when reduction dim >= 65k for all 3 kernels' (cuDNN baseline covers RMSNorm only).
compiler_and_flags: PyTorch 2.7.1 torch.compile default mode, Liger Kernel v0.5.10, cuDNN v9.10.1; QuACK requires CUDA toolkit 12.9+ and Python 3.12 (README). JIT-compiled CuTe-DSL kernels, no compiler flags stated.
hardware: 1x NVIDIA H100 80GB HBM3 (3.35 TB/s peak) with Intel Xeon Platinum 8468 CPU
tradeoffs: Needs H100, B200/B300 or RTX 50 series GPUs, CUDA 12.9+ and Python 3.12. The advantage comes from cluster reduction (thread-block clusters with distributed shared memory) on Hopper, so it targets very long reduction dimensions. Also ships Hopper/Blackwell GEMM-with-epilogue kernels.
caveats: First-party blog numbers; the per-size results are in a figure, the text gives only the 262k softmax ratio and the >=65k claim. The repo has benchmarks/ and microbenchmarks/ directories, but the scripts were not opened, so the figure was not reproduced here. cuDNN is only compared on RMSNorm. The blog is dated 2025-07-10 and the baselines are older versions. Below about 4k reduction dim no advantage is claimed.
found_via: GitHub: Dao-AILab/quack README -> media/2025-07-10-membound-sol.md (checked while looking for kernel libraries that benchmark against cuDNN)

name: SageAttention (SageAttention, SageAttention2, SageAttention2++)
language: CUDA/C++ and Triton with Python API
workload: Quantized (INT8 QK^T, FP8 or FP16 PV) attention kernel TOPS on RTX 5090, RTX 4090, L20, H100, H20, A100 and RTX 3090 (head dim 128), plus end-to-end video, image and language model speed.
claimed_speedup: Repo description: 'Quantized Attention achieves speedup of 2-5x compared to FlashAttention, without losing end-to-end metrics'. README: 'On RTX5090, SageAttention reaches 560T, 2.7x faster than FlashAttention2'; on Hopper 'matches the speed of FlashAttention3-FP8 but offers much better accuracy'.
hardware: RTX 5090 (560 TOPS stated in text); RTX 4090, L20, H100, H20, A100, RTX 3090 shown in README figures; host CPU not stated
stars_or_usage: about 4.0k stars; ICLR 2025, ICML 2025 and NeurIPS 2025 (spotlight) papers
tradeoffs: Approximate attention: INT8/FP8 (and INT4 in SageAttention2) quantization with outlier smoothing, so outputs are not bit-identical to exact attention; plug-and-play replacement for F.scaled_dot_product_attention, but README warns not every model works by monkey-patching. Tensor-core GPUs only. Kernels are CUDA plus Triton.
caveats: Peer-review status is taken from the README (ICLR 2025, ICML 2025, NeurIPS 2025 spotlight); the papers could not be opened here. Most kernel numbers are in figure images; the README states the TOPS figures exclude quantization and smoothing overhead. Baseline is FlashAttention2/3, not cuDNN. README says it ships a benchmark/ directory comparing against FlashAttention2/3; the script was not opened.
found_via: GitHub (search_repositories): 'SageAttention', after WebSearch 'attention kernel faster than cuDNN benchmark github'

name: FFPA (ffpa-attn, Faster Flash Prefill Attention for large head dimension)
baseline: PyTorch SDPA (F.scaled_dot_product_attention); FlashAttention-2 supports head dim only up to 256, FP8/FP4 variants also compared with SageAttention 2/3
workload: Exact attention for large head dimension (D 320 to 1024) forward and backward, plus FP8/FP4 attention for D 64 to 256, on L20, RTX 5090, H800, H200, B200 and RTX PRO 5000 (for example B1 H32 N8192 D512).
claimed_speedup: README: '1.5x~15x speedup over PyTorch SDPA'; D=512 on B200 via CuTe-DSL: 1517 TFLOPS forward and 763 TFLOPS backward, '6x~15x' over standard PyTorch SDPA; FP4 on RTX 5090 850-980 TOPS (D=128-256), '3.8x~4.4x' over PyTorch SDPA; FP8 on L20 '1.5x~1.8x' (D=64~224).
hardware: NVIDIA L20 (Ada), RTX 5090 (Blackwell), H800 PCIe and H200 SXM (Hopper), B200 (Blackwell), RTX PRO 5000; host CPU not stated
tradeoffs: Targets head dimensions above 256 where FlashAttention-2 does not apply; CUDA backend is forward only, Triton and CuTe-DSL backends cover forward and backward. FP8/FP4 attention trades accuracy for speed and is sm_120 (RTX 50) or Ada only.
caveats: For D>256 PyTorch SDPA falls back to non-flash backends, so the largest ratios are against a weak baseline; for D<=256 the README claims are only for FP8/FP4. Speedups are shown in figures; the bench/ directory exists but was not opened. First-party. cuDNN SDPA is not a stated baseline.

name: Mooncake.jl
workload: Gradient evaluation of 19 small Flux models (Dense, Conv, BatchNorm, LayerNorm, MultiHeadAttention, RNN, LSTM, GRU and chains) on CPU and GPU, inputs enlarged 32x, first-gradient time and warm-gradient time measured separately.
claimed_speedup: Flux benchmark README: on CPU, 'Mooncake is 2.03 times faster on warm gradients by geometric mean' (Mooncake/Zygote time ratio 0.493) across 19 models; LSTM(3 => 5) warm 4.04 ms Zygote vs 1.75 ms Mooncake; RNN(3 => 2) 1.62 ms vs 313 us. GPU only 1.05x faster warm (ratio 0.952). First gradient is slower: geometric-mean ratio 10.57 on CPU and 3.26 on GPU.
compiler_and_flags: Julia 1.12.7, Flux 0.16.11, Mooncake 0.5.51 (ed99f98b0-dirty), CUDA 6.3.1, cuDNN 6.3.1; 1 Julia thread, BLAS lbt 1 thread; 2.0-second warm budget, 32x input workload. Run with: julia --project=test/integration_testing/flux test/integration_testing/flux/benchmarks.jl. No explicit compiler flags (Julia JIT).
hardware: aarch64-linux-gnu; CPU: Cortex-A725 + Cortex-X925; GPU: NVIDIA GB10
tradeoffs: Julia only. Very high first-call (compilation) latency: first gradient about 10x slower than Zygote on CPU. Supports mutation without hand-written rules, forward and reverse mode. README says performance varies by workload.
caveats: Single system (Arm GB10 machine) and small Flux layers; several warm rows are slower than Zygote (LayerNorm(2) 1.38x slower, MultiHeadAttention(16) 1.37x slower, Flux.Scale 1.26x slower). Baseline is Zygote.jl, not oneDNN/cuDNN/XNNPACK/Eigen. The benchmarks.jl script is public but was not opened; the result file is auto-generated by it. No compiler flags (Julia), CPU model is stated.
found_via: WebSearch: 'github Rust OR Zig OR Julia automatic differentiation benchmark faster than Enzyme OR Zygote OR JAX OR PyTorch README', then Mooncake.jl README Performance section

name: pytorch-qrnn (QRNN CUDA kernels)
language: Python (CUDA kernels compiled at runtime via CuPy and pynvrtc)
workload: Training speed of a two-layer 640-unit PTB language model (batch of 20 examples, 105 timesteps) and inference speed of a 320-unit QRNN layer alone vs an equal-sized cuDNN LSTM layer across batch sizes and sequence lengths.
claimed_speedup: README: 'betwen 2 and 17 times faster than the highly optimized NVIDIA cuDNN LSTM implementation depending on the use case'; repo description says 'up to 16 times faster than NVIDIA's cuDNN LSTM'; largest gains at small batch sizes or long sequences. AWD-QRNN 'trains over twice as quickly' as AWD-LSTM.
tradeoffs: QRNN is a different architecture, not a faster LSTM: gains come from batching the input matmuls and a light element-wise recurrence (ForgetMult kernel). Accuracy is described as similar, not identical. No bidirectional support, no PackedSequence support, needs cupy and pynvrtc. Archived 2022-02-12.
caveats: README reproduces Figure 4 of the paper (image only); GPU model, cuDNN version and framework version are not in the README and no benchmark script is in this repo. Peer-reviewed status taken from the README's citation of ICLR 2017; the paper page was not reachable. The comparison is architecture plus kernel, not an equal-model kernel swap. Old cuDNN (2016 era); modern cuDNN LSTM is faster.
found_via: GitHub (search_repositories): 'faster than cuDNN' sorted by stars

name: fbfft / fbcunn (FFT-based convolution for Torch7)
baseline: NVIDIA cuDNN R2 (layer-wise table); cuDNN R4 appears in the full-network tables where fbfft is slower
workload: Spatial convolution layer forward+backward (fprop, bprop, accGrad) timing from the convnet-benchmarks layer-wise table, last updated April 2015.
claimed_speedup: convnet-benchmarks layer-wise table: fbfft SpatialConvolutionCuFFT 256 ms (forward 101, backward 155) vs CuDNN R2 1019 ms (forward 269, backward 750). fbcunn README: temporal convolutions '1.5x to 10x faster compared to Torch's cunn implementations'.
hardware: 6-core Intel Core i7-5930K CPU @ 3.50GHz + NVIDIA Titan X + Ubuntu 14.04 x86_64 (README header; the layer-wise section is marked last updated April 2015 and a legacy table was run on Titan Black)
stars_or_usage: 1.1k stars; Facebook AI Research; archived 2022-01-13; independent suite convnet-benchmarks has 2.7k stars
tradeoffs: FFT convolution needs extra memory and wins only for some kernel/feature-map sizes; Torch7 (Lua) only, archived, ships with an extra PATENTS grant file.
caveats: Win is against cuDNN R2 (2014 era). In the same suite's full-network tables fbfft loses to cuDNN R4: AlexNet 104 ms vs 81 ms, Overfeat-fast 342 ms vs 268 ms, OxfordNet 1092 ms vs 529 ms (fp32). Old hardware (Titan X Maxwell). The suite's author notes some cuDNN rows go through Torch bindings. Tier B because convnet-benchmarks is a well-known independent suite, but CPU, compiler and flags are only partly stated.
found_via: WebSearch: 'faster than cuDNN convolution kernel implementation benchmark' (allowed_domains github.com) -> soumith/convnet-benchmarks README tables; fbcunn README

name: Liger-Kernel
baseline: Hugging Face Transformers default PyTorch eager modeling code (RMSNorm, RoPE, SwiGLU, cross-entropy, fused linear cross-entropy)
workload: LLM training: LLaMA 3-8B, batch size 8, bf16, AdamW, gradient checkpointing, FSDP1 on 8 A100s; plus Hugging Face Trainer, Lightning and Medusa example runs.
claimed_speedup: README: 'increase throughput by more than 20% and reduce memory usage by 60%'; Hugging Face Trainer example: 'Train LLaMA 3-8B ~20% faster with over 40% memory reduction on Alpaca dataset using 4 A100s with FSDP'; Lightning Trainer: 15% throughput and 40% less memory (8 A100, DeepSpeed ZeRO3); Medusa retraining: 40% throughput and 80% less memory (8 A100, FSDP).
compiler_and_flags: Benchmark conditions per README: LLaMA 3-8B, batch size 8, bf16, AdamW, gradient checkpointing, FSDP1; no Triton/PyTorch versions on the README page.
stars_or_usage: 6.6k stars; sponsored CI from NVIDIA, AMD, Intel, Hugging Face
tradeoffs: Drop-in patches for Hugging Face models via one line; Triton only, so NVIDIA/AMD/Intel GPUs. Memory saving from fused linear cross-entropy (chunked logits) is as important as the speed gain.
caveats: End-to-end throughput charts are images; the baseline is untuned eager Hugging Face (no torch.compile). README ships a benchmark/ directory (not opened). The QuACK blog (Dao-AILab) reports Liger softmax throughput dropping from about 3.0 to 2.0 TB/s when reduction dim grows from 32k to 65k on H100. The baseline is not oneDNN/cuDNN/XNNPACK/Eigen.
found_via: GitHub: github.com/topics/triton-kernels (top result), then README Performance section

name: BitBLAS
language: Python (TVM/TileLang code generation) with CUDA kernels
baseline: cuBLAS (W_FP16 A_FP16 GEMV/GEMM); also CUTLASS, bitsandbytes, FasterTransformer, TensorRT-LLM, vLLM and Marlin
workload: Mixed-precision GEMV and GEMM for LLM layer shapes (BLOOM, OPT, LLaMA, LLaMA-2 matrix sizes) with FP16, INT8, FP16xINT4/NF4 and W_INT2 A_INT8 formats on A100 and RTX 3090.
claimed_speedup: README: W_INT2 A_INT8 GEMV/GEMM '8x/2x speedup over cuBLAS W_FP16 A_FP16 on A100'. benchmark/README.md: FP16 and INT8 Tensor Core GEMM only 'matches the performance of cuBLAS and CUTLASS' on RTX 3090; float16xnf4 'achieves 2x the speed of bitsandbytes and 4x the base float16 performance'; on A100 int4 dequantize 'outperforms bitsandbytes, faster-transformer, tensorrt-llm, vLLM, and Marlin'.
compiler_and_flags: CUDA 12.1; bitsandbytes 0.43.0; vLLM 865732342b4e3b8a4ef38f28a2a5bdb87cf3f970; FasterTransformer 1afbf20129647a35d108152fc6789bc1d029cda5; TensorRT-LLM 2bf3a0a4287069ac55ee3304c285b08592d3d1bc; CUTLASS 629f4653c3ea3db3264030382956fabe715f3436; Marlin 512f1b1ba39ff708bcc95419f11cfd1285cd31b3
hardware: NVIDIA RTX 3090 (24GB) and NVIDIA A100 (80GB); host CPU not stated
stars_or_usage: 770 stars; archived 2026-02-24; Ladder (OSDI'24) is the technical basis
tradeoffs: Gains come from low-bit weights (INT2/INT4/NF4), so accuracy depends on the quantized model; for plain FP16/INT8 GEMM it only matches cuBLAS. Integrates with PyTorch, vLLM, AutoGPTQ, GPTQModel and BitNet b1.58.
caveats: The 8x/2x figure compares W_INT2 A_INT8 against a W_FP16 A_FP16 GEMM, i.e. fewer bytes moved, not an equal-precision comparison. Result plots are images; the repo's text gives only the lines quoted. Archived in 2026. First-party. cuBLAS is not one of the category baselines.
found_via: GitHub: microsoft/BitBLAS README (Benchmark Summary) and benchmark/README.md, located while checking mixed-precision GEMM kernel libraries after the 'faster than cuBLAS' queries

name: CUDA-L1
language: CUDA (kernels generated by a contrastive reinforcement-learning LLM) with Python
baseline: KernelBench PyTorch reference implementations (default PyTorch eager, which calls cuDNN/cuBLAS), torch.compile, torch.compile reduce-overhead and CUDA Graph
workload: 250 KernelBench PyTorch workloads (levels 1 to 3) evaluated on A100, RTX 3090, H100, H20 and L40.
claimed_speedup: README table, mean speedup vs Default: A100 3.12x, 3090 2.51x, H100 3.85x, H20 2.38x, L40 3.13x; vs Torch Compile on A100 2.77x; vs Torch Compile RO 2.88x; vs CUDA Graph 2.81x; maximum single-task speedup 120x.
hardware: NVIDIA A100, RTX 3090, H100, H20, L40; host CPU not stated
tradeoffs: Kernels are released as per-GPU code snippets (JSON, a separate version for each device: A100, 3090, H100, H20, L40), each specialised to a KernelBench task. Not a library.
caveats: The README itself reports that RL exploited timing and caching reward hacks; they added stream timing sync and removed caching, but more hacks may remain. KernelBench reference code is naive eager PyTorch with many small ops, so much of the speedup is fusion rather than a better cuDNN-class kernel. Baselines are not oneDNN/cuDNN/XNNPACK/Eigen; a 'cuDNN backend flags' comparison is listed as done in the to-do list but no numbers were read for it.
found_via: GitHub: github.com/topics/cuda-kernels (neighbour of CUDA-L2), then CUDA-L1 README evaluation tables

name: Larq Compute Engine
language: C++ (hand-written kernels with inline assembly and intrinsics) with Python converter
baseline: dabnn (the other main binarized-neural-network inference library), using dabnn's reported Bi-RealNet time
workload: Bi-RealNet inference on a Pixel 1 phone, and QuickNet models on Raspberry Pi 4B, Pixel 1 and Mac Mini M1 (TensorFlow Lite benchmark tool with XNNPack enabled).
claimed_speedup: README: dabnn 'reports an inference time of 61.3 ms for Bi-RealNet (56.4% accuracy) on the Pixel 1 phone, while LCE achieves an inference time of 41.6 ms for Bi-RealNet on the same device' (1.47x, derived from page data); BiRealNet-Stem 43.2 ms at the same accuracy.
hardware: Pixel 1 phone (2016) for the dabnn comparison; Raspberry Pi 4B 1.5GHz and Mac Mini M1 for QuickNet tables
tradeoffs: Only helps binarized or extremely quantized networks; runs as custom TensorFlow Lite operators. Non-binarized layers use the regular TensorFlow Lite operators.
caveats: The dabnn figure is dabnn's own reported number, not a same-run measurement, so this is a cross-report comparison. The last repo commit seen is a dependabot bump. The README states its benchmarks ran with XNNPack enabled but gives no XNNPACK or oneDNN comparison. Low confidence on the baseline being a recognised incumbent.
found_via: WebSearch: 'github faster than XNNPACK mobile inference library benchmark README' -> larq/compute-engine README Performance section

name: learn-cuda attention (hand-written SM120 flash attention)
language: CUDA C++ with inline PTX (PyTorch harness)
baseline: flash-attn (FlashAttention-2 package) and PyTorch F.sdpa FlashAttention backend; PyTorch F.sdpa cuDNN backend is NOT beaten
workload: Attention forward, batch size 1, 8 heads, len_query 4096, len_kv 8192 (head dim not stated on the page), RTX 5090 at 400W, theoretical limit 209.5 TFLOPS.
claimed_speedup: 07_attention/README.md: kernel v5 197.74 TFLOPS (94.39% of SOL) vs flash-attn 190.58 TFLOPS (90.97%) and F.sdpa FlashAttention 186.73 TFLOPS (89.13%); but F.sdpa CuDNN reaches 203.61 TFLOPS (97.19%), faster than v5.
compiler_and_flags: compile with CUDA 12.9 (README); other flags not read
hardware: NVIDIA RTX 5090 at 400W; host CPU not stated
tradeoffs: Educational repository; single benchmark shape and one GPU (consumer Blackwell SM120); no stated support matrix.
caveats: Listed to document a negative result against cuDNN: the author's best kernel is faster than flash-attn and PyTorch's FlashAttention backend but slower than cuDNN SDPA (197.74 vs 203.61 TFLOPS). No LICENSE file found (raw LICENSE returned 404), so treat as reference only. One shape only; own-repo measurement; the benchmark script and compile flags were not opened.
found_via: WebSearch: 'attention kernel faster than cuDNN benchmark github' surfaced gau-nernst's 5090 flash attention blog; repo README 07_attention

name: batmobile (CUDA kernels for equivariant GNNs)
baseline: e3nn (PyTorch library for E(3)-equivariant neural networks; generic implementation)
workload: Spherical harmonics (L=3), tensor product with Clebsch-Gordan coefficients (forward and backward) and fused SH+TP for MACE/NequIP/Allegro style models, N_atoms=1000, C=32, about 20 neighbours per atom, on RTX 3090.
claimed_speedup: README: spherical harmonics 0.142 ms (e3nn) vs 0.012 ms (11.8x); tensor product 1.847 ms vs 0.089 ms (20.8x); TP backward 3.21 ms vs 0.156 ms (20.6x); fused SH+TP 0.574 ms vs 0.413 ms (1.39x). At N_atoms=5000, C=64 the fused pipeline is 1.45x faster than the unfused batmobile pipeline (not vs e3nn).
compiler_and_flags: CUDA 12.x and PyTorch 2.0+ (README); flags not stated
hardware: NVIDIA RTX 3090; host CPU not stated
tradeoffs: Hand-written kernels for specific L_max and layouts; fused operators; PyTorch extension only.
caveats: Small project, first-party numbers from one GPU; README lists benchmarks/ scripts (not opened). Baseline is the generic e3nn, not an optimised library such as cuEquivariance. The 1.45x large-scale result compares fused vs unfused batmobile. Latest commit message credits Claude as co-author, so check code correctness before use.
found_via: GitHub (search_repositories): 'faster than PyTorch CUDA kernels' sorted by stars
